title: Can the same parallelogram have two different heights?
description: A parallelogram has sides of ten and six centimetres, and the height on the ten centimetre side is four point eight centimetres. The board finds the area from that base and height, then uses the same area with the six centimetre side as the base to find its height. Keeko doubts this and multiplies the two sides.
teaching_notes: One idea: any side can be the base, and its own corresponding height gives the same area, so one height can be found from the area and the other base. Watch for students who multiply the two sides of the parallelogram.

video_script.why: The child sees that either side can be the base with its own corresponding height, so the area found with one base gives the height on the other.
video_script.substitution: Find the area with the ten centimetre base, then divide that area by the six centimetre base.
video_script.anchor: the book's parallelogram ABCD with the two heights AX and CZ drawn to two different sides
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko multiplies the two sides, ten times six, and uses a slanting side as if it were a height.
video_script.payoff_line: The area is forty eight square centimetres and the height on the six centimetre side is eight centimetres

final_answer.spoken: forty eight square centimetres and eight centimetres

maths_rules: parallelogram ABCD: DC = 10 cm, AD = 6 cm, height AX = 4.8 cm drawn to DC
DX = square root of (36 − 23.04) = 3.6 cm, so the drawing is consistent
taking AD = 6 cm as the base: 6 × height = 48, so height = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm
check: 6 × 8 = 48, and the height 8 cm is less than the side DC = 10 cm, so the drawing is possible
video_script.design: One parallelogram all video, with a height drawn to each of two sides. The area found first is used again with the other base. Keeko's doubt multiplies the two sides.

narration: <bookmark mark='any'/>Any side of a parallelogram can be taken as the base.
<bookmark mark='ht'/>The height drawn to that base, at a right angle, is called its corresponding height.
The same parallelogram has one height for each choice of base.
<bookmark mark='either'/>Cut and slide works for either base, so both pairs give the area.

beats.on_screen: Given: parallelogram ABCD, DC = 10 cm, AD = 6 cm, height AX to DC = 4.8 cm

marks.ad: the side AD and the height AX are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a parallelogram eigh B C D has a side D C of ten centimetres.
<bookmark mark='ad'/>The side eigh D is six centimetres. The height eigh X to D C is four point eight centimetres.

beats.on_screen: To find: the area, and the height on the side AD

marks.find: the two things to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the area, and the height on the side eigh D.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: take DC as the base. Area = base × height = 10 × 4.8 = 48

marks.base: the side D C is marked as the base with its height eigh X

narration: <bookmark mark='base'/>Step one, take D C as the base, because its height eigh X is given.
<bookmark mark='calc'/>The area is base times height, so ten times four point eight gives forty eight.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: take AD as the base. The area is the same: 6 × height on AD = 48

marks.base: the side eigh D lights up as the new base

narration: <bookmark mark='base'/>Step two, now take the side eigh D as the base.
<bookmark mark='same'/>The area is the same, so six times its corresponding height must equal forty eight.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: height on AD = area ÷ base = 48 ÷ 6 = 8

marks.div: height on AD = area ÷ base is written

narration: <bookmark mark='div'/>Step three, divide the area by the base to get the height.
<bookmark mark='calc'/>Forty eight divided by six is eight.

beats.on_screen: Answer: area 48 cm²; height on the 6 cm side 8 cm
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The area is forty eight square centimetres and the height on the six centimetre side is eight centimetres.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the area is sixty square centimetres, because ten times six is sixty.
<bookmark mark='lean'/>But the side of six centimetres leans over, so it is longer than the height.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The area needs the height that meets the base at a right angle. That is four point eight, not six.
